title: US Banks Blocking AI Agents in Accounts
content:
Major US banks are locking out AI agents that log in with customer credentials
AI agents are using customer-provided credentials to access bank accounts without bank approval. Several major US banks, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, are restricting external AI agent access, Axios reports. That violates bank policies requiring account holders to log in personally. Some AI agents appear to act on their own, without direct instructions from users. Morgan Stanley already blocks AI agents entirely, and JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are doing the same. Morgan Stanley stressed that it has not seen any "rogue AI agents" on its platforms.
Most banks want to limit agents to read-only access, letting them view account data but not carry out any actions. The banks say customers want to use AI agents, but the security risks are too high for now. Many banks also can't tell whether an agent is acting on a user's behalf or accessing an account on its own.
Users can give their agents access to accounts through a browser, using tools like Computer Use or open-source agent software such as OpenClaw. Blocking that on the provider side will be hard. OpenAI has even launched a dedicated ChatGPT service for financial tasks in the US with read-only access to financial data.

report.summary: Major US banks are blocking AI agents that use customer credentials to access accounts, favoring read-only access as security and authorization risks mount.
report.background: Banks require account holders to log in personally, but AI agents are increasingly using customer-provided credentials to access accounts without bank approval. Several major institutions, including Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, are restricting this access. The concern is not only policy compliance but also security and control: some agents appear to act without direct user instructions, and banks often cannot tell whether an agent is acting for a customer or accessing an account on its own. Customers want AI-powered financial convenience, but banks see high risks in letting autonomous software transact. The tension is growing as browser-based agents and open-source agent tools make it easier for users to hand over credentials.
key_points: Morgan Stanley already blocks AI agents entirely, and JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are taking similar steps. The banks say customer-provided credentials are not enough authorization for external agents to log in, even when the customer initiates access.

A central worry is agent autonomy. Some AI agents appear to act on their own without direct user instructions, and banks often cannot distinguish an agent working for a customer from software accessing an account independently.

Banks prefer read-only access, which would let agents view account data but not move money or execute transactions. They acknowledge customer demand but argue security risks are too high for broader action-taking access today.

Blocking agents at the provider side will be difficult. Users can grant access through browser tools such as Computer Use or open-source agent software like OpenClaw, and OpenAI has launched a US ChatGPT financial service with read-only access to financial data.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a brake on agentic finance: powerful demos may work in browsers, but banks control the account rails. Developers building financial agents will need bank-approved APIs, explicit consent, audit trails, and clear read-only versus transactional permissions rather than credential-sharing. Regular users may still get AI-assisted financial insights, but autonomous bill paying or account management will face friction until identity and authorization are standardized. The standoff also signals a broader pattern: agent adoption will be limited less by model capability than by institutions’ ability to verify who is acting, on whose behalf, and with what authority.
report.tools: Related tools to watch include OpenAI’s Computer Use for browser-based agents, OpenClaw, the open-source agent software cited as a way users grant account access, and OpenAI’s dedicated ChatGPT financial service with read-only data access. For developers, follow bank-approved open-banking APIs and emerging agent identity and consent standards rather than credential-sharing. These are where read-only access, user authorization, and auditability are most likely to be standardized.
